items.body: The reason I like John Coltrane’s Concert in Japan best out of all my Coltrane albums is that it includes one of my all-time favorite tracks: “Peace on Earth”. And as good as “Meditation/Leo (Part One),” “Leo (Part Two),” and “Part Three” are - “Peace on Earth” outshines them all. When John Coltrane arrived in Japan in 1966, he was welcomed like a king. He arrived at Haneda Airport on July 8, 1966, along with his wife Alice, Pharoah Sanders, Jimmy Garrison, and Rashied Ali. Ali, who later recalled the trip, said they were greeted by thousands of Japanese fans. At the airport, there were huge, life-size cardboard cutouts of the musicians, a red carpet leading from the plane to the terminal, and bouquets of flowers. And Coltrane had a message, it was no coincidence that he wanted to perform in Japan. He insisted on traveling to Nagasaki to visit the Peace Memorial at the site of the atomic bombing. He laid down a wreath and prayed for a long time. The place had a profound emotional and spiritual impact on him. On the evening of his concert in Nagasaki, he played “Peace on Earth” - at that time a new piece and a kind of musical prayer for peace. At a press conference during the tour, when asked about the Vietnam War, he said: “I dislike war, period. It should stop, and any other war.” On Concert in Japan - and on “Peace on Earth” in particular - one can see how Coltrane’s thirst for new sounds is inextricably linked to his desire to view the universe from a spiritual perspective; his music radiates a cosmic aura. The piece begins with an incredibly beautiful melody that floats above Alice’s arpeggios, Garrison’s bass sprinklings, and Ali’s sparse drumming. It seems like the musical embodiment of the Garden of Eden. Nearly six minutes of pure harmony - but then deliberate atonality creeps in, paradise is threatened, only heavenly saxophone lines save it for the time being. Then, however, a dissonant storm is conjured up, shaking this world to its very foundations. The piece is thrown into utter disarray; block chords replace the arpeggios, and the bass and drums throw the meter overboard. At the very end, however, harmony returns, and the melodies resurface, albeit different from how they began. In July 1966, John Coltrane was just one year away from his untimely death, yet his zest for life was greater than ever. His musical explorations were more adventurous than before, and “Peace on Earth” brilliantly captures the essence of what his music is all about. Or, as my friend Thomas Weber puts it: “On the one hand, it’s utter extravagance and exhaustion, on the other, it’s the dissolution of boundaries. Free jazz with melodies.” Email This BlogThis! items._cn_summary: 这张专辑记录了约翰·柯川1966年访日期间的现场演出，其中《Peace on Earth》是乐评人最为推崇的作品。柯川赴日前特意前往长崎和平纪念公园献花祈祷，使这首作品成为一曲祈求和平的音乐祷文。演出阵容包括爱丽丝·柯川、费罗·桑德斯、Jimmy Garrison与Rashied Ali。《Peace on Earth》起始于一段优美的旋律，漂浮于爱丽丝的琶音、Garrison稀疏的低音点缀与Ali稀疏的鼓点之上，约六分钟后刻意的不和谐音逐渐渗透，乐园受到威胁，不和谐的风暴彻底颠覆节奏与和声，最终旋律以变形的形态回归。乐评指出，柯川对新声音的渴求与其从精神层面观察宇宙的愿望密不可分，音乐散发宇宙气息，既是极致的放纵与耗尽，也是边界的消融——带有旋律的自由爵士。

items.body: Canadian electronic and experimental composer Tim Hecker is dropping his ninth solo album, Konoyo, on September 28 through Kranky, and it comes after the label’s reissuing and remastering of his earlier Haunt Me, Haunt Me, Do It Again and Radio Amor. Konoyo’s soul is rooted in Japan, where, in a temple on the outskirts of Tokyo, Hecker collaborated with members from the Gagaku Ensemble Tokyo Gakuso, gagaku being an ancient form of Japanese classical music – ‘elegant music’ – performed for many centuries at the Imperial Court. As a result, Konoyo offers an immediate change of mood. Konoyo is a response. Concerned with negative space and a continued concern for music’s ‘increasingly banal density’, Konoyo’s timbre is one of constriction, its mood sombre, akin to a lost kingdom and a crown that’s faded from its once-burnt gold. Strings are stretched to breaking point, but they’re still able to shine with a dull radiance, are still beautiful in their crystalline gleaming and their cavernous echoes, managing to sound strangely harmonious even in ongoing anguish. The sound is refined in its elegant, controlled falls, its growling low tones and rivers of grit; its squeals of unease and dissatisfaction are similar in tone to the inky darkness of Ravedeath, 1972. Tracks pick up extra tonal layers along the way, and they suddenly populate the music, clanking thickly with the heavy air of ceremony. On ‘Keyed Out’, the track mutates halfway in, starting off in menacing territory, segueing into a quiet stretch where nothing moves, before adding in an array of electronic sounds. The album addresses decay – which, in the physical world, is inevitable – but it’s more to do with the decay of a crushed spirit, examining a growing dissatisfaction with music in its current state and the falling away of all things. In Konoyo, something is failing, something is struggling; burning out. And because of that, it feels radically different, at times tired and at other times angry, and thus alive. As they slow down, the notes lose some of their vitality, energy draining like a spent battery, becoming dense glitch-hieroglyphics and mirage-like squares; you have to squint in order to see them. But the sounds are still able to gleam, shining like the sharp blade of a katana in the dark, a brandished sliver of light in a black cage. The tones seem to be running wild – multiple sources overlap, crushing others, but they never feel like they’re in competition with one another – and Hecker tempers the numerous sounds to great effect, retaining a crestfallen mood inside its tight locket despite the occasional rush-hours within the record. In September, the regal sense of decay is given extra emphasis. Autumn, when nature relinquishes, sleeps, and dies with a bang, a flourishing display of might and majesty. Similar things happen in the darkened labyrinth of Konoyo’s temple, its reverent music dominated by a pervasive feeling of tilted discord and ambient loss. Dissolving like sodium, like acid rain pounding the street, the music glows like a halogen, offering a wink of light and nothing more; refusing to offer more. The thumping, slow-bleeding percussion on closing track ‘Across to Anoyo’ is strong at first, but even this succumbs and dissolves, eroding like a corpse in its coffin. The ennui is pervasive. Despite its restrictions, Konoyo is more than generous. Its long running time and its spectacular tonal array is something of a wonder, untameable as always, even if its mood is adamantly downcast. Hecker will stage a series of special performances in tandem with the album’s release, featuring members of the Gagaku ensemble on sh?, ryuteki and hichiriki, accompanied by Kara-Lis Coverdale. Live dates: Oct 2 – Tokyo WWWX Oct 6 – London Barbican Oct 7 – Krakow Unsound Oct 8 – Berlin Funkhaus www.kranky.net www.timhecker.bandcamp.com
items._genre: experimental electronic / ambient drone / Japanese gagaku fusion / dark ambient
items._cn_summary: Tim Hecker 第九张个人专辑与东京郊外寺庙的雅乐乐团合作完成，将古老的日本宫廷雅乐引入电子与失谐音景的语境。专辑以极简的负空间、压缩的音色和缓慢衰变的质感为核心，弦线在临界点上拉伸却仍维持微弱光泽，低频咆哮与细碎颗粒交织成仪式感的沉重空气。多层音色叠覆却不互相竞争，整体笼罩在衰败王国的庄重氛围中。专辑回应当代音乐日益平庸的密集化倾向，以沉思与疲倦的姿态探询精神的瓦解与燃烧，既是对音乐现状的不满，也是对一切消逝的哀悼。Kranky 厂牌发行延续了独立实验脉络，与 Hecker 此前被再版的早期作品形成纵向互文。

items.body: Black album covers are fairly rare; Prince’s The Black Album comes to mind, along with Thembi Soddell’s black-on-black Love Songs, which includes a book of black print on black pages. Rachel Shearer is the latest addition to this small group, as Te Oro a te Ao (the resounding of the world) presents black type on a black background. The hue honors Hinenuitepō, the goddess of night and death, and issues a warning on climate change. Shearer reflects her Aotearoan (New Zealand) roots by translating the Māori concept of whakapapa into aural form. The belief that all of nature, including time, is connected forms the basis of this work. The opening “Waha” (featuring Cathy Livermore) means both gate and voice, and serves as an entry point not only to the album, but to the spiritual world. It arrives as an invocation or incantation, at first a cappella, then layered, then sanded with dirt, dust and rock. Over time it becomes a choir, its sedimentary layers accumulating until they solidify into a drone. Is this the earth speaking, or our ancestors, or the buzz of time? The collective sound overtakes the individual without sublimating her power. The heart of the album is the two-part “Pounamu Becoming Crystal.” The first part reflects the “movement and strength of water,” which begins as a mist yet transforms into a torrent. While experiencing such dynamic contrast, one may think of everything from the act of creation to the destruction of the planet. The piece incorporates “subterranean volcanic activity, tectonic plate movements and land slippages,” and acts as a parable of disruption. Yet by the end, the timbres soften, offering a modicum of hope; perhaps time’s arrow is instead a cycle. The second segment, subtitled “Wiriwiri” (to tremble), honors the dance of Tānerore: the visible shimmer of hot air as it rises from the ground. At first, the piece continues the rumbling timbres of its predecessor, but these give way to white noise: the processed sound of cicadas, whose volume increases with the temperature. As Earth warms, the cries of the cicadas grow ever more insistent. “Ao” is a flexible word that can mean “sunrise,” “clouds” or even “world.” This gentle guitar coda suggests a manner of living on the planet, honoring sound with sound, presence with presence, gift with gift. While this is the Māori way, it is not often replicated, especially in Western societies. The arc of the album – invitation, experience, farewell – suggests a mode of interaction that posits all creation, animate and inanimate, as partners, the breath of heat mingling with the breath of life, the audible with the inaudible, the present with the absent and the yet-to-come. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: ambient / experimental / world fusion / drone
items._cn_summary: Rachel Shearer 的专辑《Te Oro a te Ao》以黑色封面向黑夜女神 Hinenuitepō 致敬，同时警示气候变化危机。她将毛利人的"whakapapa"（万物相连）观念转化为听觉形式，贯穿全作的核心理念是自然、时间与生命的彼此交织。开场曲"Waha"（意为门与声音）从清唱开始，逐步叠加并混入泥土、尘埃与岩石的质感声响，最终汇聚成持续音，仿佛大地、祖先与时间本身的低语。核心曲目"Pounamu Becoming Crystal"分两部分：第一部分以水汽到洪流的剧烈动态变化隐喻创造与毁灭，融入火山活动与地壳运动的实地录音；第二部分以蝉鸣的白噪音呈现温度升高带来的生态紧迫感。终曲"Ao"以轻柔吉他收束，暗示一种与星球共存的呼吸方式。整张专辑构筑出邀请—体验—告别的弧线，将有声与无声、可见与不可见、现在与未来并置为合作关系。

items.body: Arcana Magna Silentia Cold Meat Industry The fourteen year gap between Swedish neo-classical/dark ambient project Arcana’s As Bright As A Thousand Suns and new LP Magna Silentia was marked by halted reactivations, live reunions, and tremendous personal loss for Peter and Cecilia Bjärgö and their collaborators. It’s no surprise, then, to find them working in a register quite different from their last recorded material, though Magna Silentia‘s combination of Arcana’s earliest and most austere work and the technical prowess they’ve since accrued makes for a striking and affecting reemergence. Records like Thousand Suns and Raspail saw an expansion of Arcana’s acoustic side, augmenting their neo-classical side with folk threads which resulted in a sound not unlike mid-period Dead Can Dance. That degree of ornamentation has been stripped back Magna Silentia. Low, abyssal horns and drones accompany ritual drums whose earthy timbre carries real menace on “The Adversity Bell”, yet the melodic thread of the piece, carried almost exclusively by Peter’s wordless vocals, is far more frail and pained than those more bracing elements might suggest. And it’s in that tension, between the severity of a record which fittingly marks Arcana’s return to Cold Meat Industry (and everything that infamous label entails) and the full, crushing emotional register of real human grief and loss, that Magna Silentia shines. A sustained focus on funereal dark ambient drones and echoes is often the conduit for that tension. Dark ambient has always been one part of Arcana’s heady alchemy to be sure, but it’s never been given so much focus as it has here. The rich sound design and subtle but elegant compositional chops which guide “Somnia Intus” might not have been achievable for Bjärgö in the project’s early years, but are now well within his grasp and fit the record’s sober and enduring grief. While perhaps more abstract and less directly emotional, “The Obsidian Mirror” again finds Arcana wielding both metallic, industrial noise and contemplative tones in equilibrium (for a project which has always focused on atmosphere they’ve rarely felt “cinematic” in the way that term’s often deployed, yet there’s something of a classic cyberpunk cityscape in this track). For all of its pain and extremity, there are real currents of beauty in Magna Silentia. The mournful violin which passes through glowing chorales in “The Collapsing Of All Light” might not be as bombastic as some of Arcana’s earlier neo-classical works, but it’s as affecting as any of them. After their hiatus Arcana have returned to their roots, shaped by time and loss, but none the weaker for it. Recommended. Buy it. Magna Silentia by Arcana The post Arcana, “Magna Silentia” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是瑞典暗潮/新古典项目Arcana在十四年沉寂后的回归之作，发表于传奇厂牌Cold Meat Industry。乐评指出作品剥离了此前专辑中类似Dead Can Dance式的民谣装饰与华丽编配，转向更克制、更沉重的方向。低沉的号角与持续低音铺垫出深渊般的氛围，仪式鼓点与Peter的无词人声形成强烈张力；暗潮漂移与回响在多首曲目中占据主导，配合金属质感的工业噪音与冥想式的音色平衡，展现出远超乐队早期作品的声响设计深度。专辑承载着乐队成员多年来的真实丧亲之痛，悲恸的小提琴穿越合唱段落，情感浓度极高。这种将早期简约美学与多年积累的复杂制作技艺相融合的做法，使专辑既是对乐队根源的回归，也是个人创伤的艺术化表达，在冰冷声响与人类情感的撕扯之间形成持续的戏剧张力。

items.body: Truth must be said from the beginning, I’m not, even a little, objective when it comes to John Coltrane’s last chapter in life and in music. Those two are inseparable in any case. Second truth is that this last period that starts roughly sometime in 1964, prior to A Love Supreme, and ends with his death is my favorite music. He and all his comrades, especially Alice, Pharoah, Rashied and Jimmy managed to create a body of music of transcendence –an ascension for the soul and deep meditation for the mind. My album of choice is this last live recording (where the aforementioned musicians are joined by Juma Santos and Algie DeWitt on percussion), recorded just three months before his death at the Olatunji Center of African Culture in Harlem, N.Y.C. In a quite symbolic move (the place: deep in an African-American neighborhood, the name: African Culture and tradition as a starting point) the music of the players, even though both geographically and in name still black, still jazz but free, is already a new entity. With this recording, one that the sound is not so hi-fi, Coltrane’s sound seems to be in the final stage of the total freedom that Ascension initiated. Listening to the unrelenting growls, howls and their thick wall of sound created by Trane and Pharoah, one could easily comment that the two tracks, Ogunde of almost half an hour and the total reconstruction of My Favorite Things that clocks in thirty four uncontrollably joyous minutes, are pure noise. This ferocious a la Ayler attack by the two locked in reeds brothers, provides a rough field, like a magic carpet flying in the air, for the others to give everything they have. And they have to give a lot to the not so big crowd attending, as their collective struggle to follow or lead at some points, or intertwine with small gestures like the polyrhythmic-not-so-rhythmic barrages by Rashied, the lovingly plucked piano chords by Alice and the even though not always audible, monstrous strength by Jimmy on double bass. Allow me to humbly comment that Coltrane’s music channeled everything in black tradition and went beyond that. He created his own tradition. You also don’t need me to say that this is an amazing recording. One that encapsulates all the stated goals by John Coltrane himself. Total freedom, love, myriads of feelings and a spiritual unity that could be the final Truth. If there’s something to think about, to question, it could be this: where could his music go after this? Did he, before even turning 41, reached a point of no return? @fot.isn Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / avant-garde / spiritual jazz / afrocentric
items._cn_summary: 这是John Coltrane临终前三个月在哈林区奥拉通吉非洲文化中心录制的现场专辑，是他音乐生涯最后阶段的见证。乐队由Alice Coltrane、Pharoah Sanders、Rashied Ali和Jimmy Garrison等核心成员组成，加入了Juma Santos和Algie DeWitt担任打击乐。两首长篇作品——近半小时的Ogunde和三十四分钟的My Favorite Things重构——展现了Coltrane与Sanders双簧管/萨克斯的密集声墙，以类似Albert Ayler式的猛烈攻击铺展即兴场域。Alice Coltrane的钢琴拨奏、Rashied Ali的多节奏冲击与Jimmy Garrison的低音贝斯在粗粝的声场中交织推进。录音音质虽不够精致，却忠实呈现了Coltrane将非裔传统与精神性追求融为一体的极致自由美学，是他追求超越与冥想的最后宣言。

items.album: [2View] Maps and Diagrams’ beneath still stars (handstitched*) & returning light (Home Normal)
items.excerpt: Two decades removed from the clockwork IDM of Polytuft-Tech, Tim Martin’s returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) find him stripping everything back to drift, texture, and quietly resonant melody, resulting in two companion albums that feel less like separate releases than different sides of the same long, unhurried thought.   Companion pieces, two sides of the same drift beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagrams   Tim M
items.body: Two decades removed from the clockwork IDM of Polytuft-Tech, Tim Martin’s returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) find him stripping everything back to drift, texture, and quietly resonant melody, resulting in two companion albums that feel less like separate releases than different sides of the same long, unhurried thought.   Companion pieces, two sides of the same drift beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagrams   Tim Martin has been Maps and Diagrams since the early 2000s, and the entry point for a lot of people into his catalog is Polytuft-Tech, released in 2003 on Expanding Records, an album that got filed under IDM, ambient, and glitch at a moment when those three words together still meant something specific and rigorous. That record ran on clicky drums that whirred like clockwork under warm, streamlined melodies. It landed near the tail end of IDM’s most experimentally saturated period, right as the genre itself was quietly transitioning into whatever came next, and it stands as one of the more melodically generous statements from that stretch. Both returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) are nowhere near that record sonically. Drums are gone almost entirely. Glitch has been replaced by drift. But it’s still unmistakably Tim, the same restrained, resonant signature that’s followed him through two decades of output, just aged into something quieter. Both albums arrive within weeks of each other on different labels with different histories attached. returning light is Home Normal‘s second release from Tim this year, following tone isolation, his actual debut on the label despite Home Normal running for over seventeen years, a gap explained by the fact that Tim‘s earliest UK work went through Nomadic Kids Republic, Home Normal‘s sister label, back in 2011 with Lights Will Call On You and The Town Beneath The Sea. beneath still stars comes out on handstitched*, the label Tim runs himself, which has carried his more private and experimental output for years alongside releases like In Circles. One album through someone else’s curatorial lens, one through his own. That distinction matters more than it initially seems to. Ambient releases should never get judged track by track in isolation. The genre works as a collective experience, an album like this either builds a sustained emotional environment across its runtime or it doesn’t, and no individual piece can really save or sink that outcome on its own. What matters more is whether the melodies that surface actually resonate, whether they invoke something specific rather than just occupying space. Both of these records succeed at that, though they do it through slightly different means. “ArcWorld-6.4 Rev.42 [sgl.break]” from beneath still stars is one of the more fascinating pieces across either release, another example of the part A / part B structure that’s shown up in other reviews recently. It connects two ideas without part B ever feeling like a continuation of part A. Instead it functions as an introduction to something entirely different, and the transition is peaceful in a way that most of this album is. The track titles throughout beneath still stars read almost like technical drafts, numbered revisions, hertz values, file extensions in brackets like [static] or [lost.wav] or [mem.void]. That naming isn’t arbitrary. It reads like an iteration system, drafts selected and refined specifically rather than titled decoratively after the fact. “Raddius.ocean-IX [r.36-04hz]” is another two-part piece, but this one connects rather than diverges, a drone-like melodic note giving way to a dreamlike synth tuned to a specific frequency, which the title tells you outright. Intentional down to the hertz. “beneath still stars and returning light aren’t competing statements, they’re companion pieces, two sides of the same drift, released close enough together that they start to feel like one long, unhurried thought that just happened to get split across two labels.” ~J. Batista A different level of drone entirely :: returning light sits in the same emotional register but sounds noticeably different sonically. There are small clicks and glitches scattered through certain tracks, and the pads and atmospheres carry a different weight than what’s happening on beneath still stars. “falling rainbows” uses static hits inside its pad environments to create reverbed textures that read almost like snare hits, except Tim‘s building that rhythmic tension entirely out of pad effects and reverb rather than anything resembling a drum sample. “just moving” introduces keys that sound almost like distortion at first before resolving into something prettier the longer you sit with it, a different level of drone entirely, since nothing here holds on a single note. There’s room for other melodies to form and enter, and they do. “somewhat virtual interactions” is a favorite, what sounds like a distorted “ahhh” vocal fragment sits so subtly in the mix that it changes the character of the pads around it, and there are field recording glitches scattered throughout that open up real space inside the track. “Open Water” plays almost like an audio representation of a shishi-odoshi—that traditional Japanese bamboo water fountain that fills, tips, empties, and resets in a slow repeating cycle. Tim‘s using effects here the same way that device uses gravity and water, building a soft, cyclical sense of rhythm entirely out of texture rather than percussion. “ouvertures” closes the album starting soft and distorted, and around the 3:55 mark a low humming frequency starts creeping in that sounds baked into the synth itself, eventually rolling and degrading the audio as the track winds down. A genuinely cool effect to end on. “Tim Martin has landed somewhere his younger self probably wasn’t building toward. Whether that’s evolution or just where two decades of making ambient music eventually deposits a person is hard to say, and probably doesn’t matter.” ~J. Batista There’s a version of this review that picks a favorite between the two records. That version would be missing the point entirely. beneath still stars and returning light aren’t competing statements, they’re companion pieces, two sides of the same drift, released close enough together that they start to feel like one long, unhurried thought that just happened to get split across two labels. beneath still stars is the more clinical of the pair. Drafted, revised, numbered like lab notes, every track title reading like a version history for a synth that never stops evolving. Twenty years removed from Polytuft-Tech‘s clockwork drums and whirring percussion, Tim Martin has landed somewhere his younger self probably wasn’t building toward. Whether that’s evolution or just where two decades of making ambient music eventually deposits a person is hard to say, and probably doesn’t matter. These two records don’t argue for themselves. They don’t need to. They just sit there, patiently, until you notice forty minutes have passed and you’ve barely moved. Home Normal got the warmer half. handstitched*—Tim‘s own label, his own house, got the rawer, more exacting one. He gets to have it both ways. So does anyone who sits with both records long enough to stop telling them apart. beneath still stars is available on handstitched* and returing light is available on Home Normal. beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagramsThe post [2View] Maps and Diagrams’ beneath still stars (handstitched*) & returning light (Home Normal) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: 乐评聚焦于Tim Martin以Maps and Diagrams之名发行的两张姊妹专辑：Home Normal厂牌的returning light与自创厂牌handstitched*的beneath still stars。乐评追溯了他从2003年Expanding Records时期Polytuft-Tech那种钟表般精密的IDM风格出发，经过二十年沉淀后彻底剥离鼓机与故障元素，转向纯粹的drift、质感纹理与低鸣旋律。两张专辑分别经由他人策展视角与自我发行渠道同期问世，前者是厂牌十七年来首次发行Tim作品的突破，后者承载其更私密与实验性的输出。乐评强调ambient类型应以整体氛围而非单曲来评判，指出两张专辑虽路径不同——一个通过解构与拼贴，另一个通过温暖的回响——却都在旋律浮现时唤起了具体的情感共鸣，共同构成同一段漫长思绪的两面。

items.body: Review by memowakeman — Review originally posted at www.therocktologist.comA third exquisite offering. The talented Italian quartet Aether is back with an incredibly solid, mature, refined, and creative album, one that fans of jazz fusion, progressive rock, and music that appeals to the senses will enjoy from beginning to end. Across 43 minutes and six tracks, the musicians treat us to a series of sonic landscapes that range from relaxing to frenetic, from atmospheric to deeply sensory, moving seamlessly between rock, post-rock, ambient, and classical music. It all begins with "Oort Cloud," whose opening seconds are atmospheric and otherworldly, creating a contemplative, dark mood. Little by little, new elements and sounds emerge, making you feel as though you are floating through space, caught somewhere between uncertainty and curiosity, until everything erupts at the 2:30 mark and a new rhythm takes over, retaining that dark sound that at times reminds me of early-70s King Crimson. As the minutes go by, the band introduces more colors, with the keyboards becoming a crucial element. Nevertheless, the atmospheres created by the bass, guitar, and drums come together to form a truly fascinating sonic experience. Next comes "Vogon," where the bass maintains a steady pulse while the guitar, keyboards, and drums appear here and there, gradually moving from uncertainty toward a sense of resolution as a distinctly jazzy melody begins to take shape. The very distinctive voice of the theatrical Claudio Milano emerges to recite a poem, creating one of the album's most unique moments. Shortly after his voice fades away, the music explodes, and jazz gives way to rock, with Andrea Ferrari's guitar charging forward like a whirlwind of emotions, compelling you to move and simply enjoy the music. The sonic landscapes shift in fascinating ways on "Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres." It begins by creating spacious, otherworldly soundscapes that, after two and a half minutes, take on an almost psychedelic essence, thanks first to the hypnotic bass of Andrea Grumelli, who guides the way as the guitar, synths, and drums deliver a daring and wonderful blend of space rock and jazz. This is one of my favorite tracks on the album. "La M�lancolie Du Petit Prince" features Andrea Serino's piano as the central element and guiding force of this literary-inspired passage. Beyond the blend of jazz and classical music brought to life by the piano, I love the fretless bass and its wonderfully fluid, graceful notes. I am also particularly fond of the deliciously sensory percussion Matteo Ravelli plays at the beginning, which he later contrasts with his electronic devices. Another majestic moment arrives with "Panta Rei." Its eight minutes unleash the quartet's imagination and creativity, showing us that after three studio albums, these musicians understand one another exceptionally well and flow together naturally, not only as accomplished instrumentalists but, more importantly, as a band. And although there are several darker, denser moments, I love the balance they achieve, as we suddenly find ourselves immersed in passages that feel bright and full of promise. At one point, they even reminded me of Focus. And yes, progressive rock is very much present here. Finally, the album reaches its brilliant conclusion with "Swerve." Over the course of its ten minutes, Aether delivers the climax of the entire work, a clear testament to the evolution of their sound and their boundless creativity. The band brings together a rich mix of genres and emotions, allowing listeners to immerse themselves in progressive passages, profound atmospheres, and enveloping, emotionally charged textures. The rhythm and intensity gradually build from the halfway point onward, creating a sonic spectrum that makes you want to move with the music, feel it, savor every moment, and truly make it your own. Congratulations to Aether on such a solid release. I absolutely loved it.
items._genre: post-rock / progressive rock / jazz fusion / math rock / ambient
items._cn_summary: 意大利四人乐队Aether的第三张录音室专辑在四十三分钟内构建了六段声音景观，从氛围化的太空漂浮感出发，逐步引入爵士律动、古典钢琴语汇与后摇爆发力。作品在松弛与狂躁之间自由切换，键盘与无品贝斯交织出流畅的对话，鼓手在原声打击与电子设备之间游走，吉他在whirlwind般的情绪释放中占据主导。曲目编排注重渐进式展开与情绪弧线，文学性标题暗示概念化构思。乐队成员经过三张专辑的磨合，展现出高度的默契，演奏既具技术深度又富即兴色彩，融合爵士、前卫摇滚、氛围与古典元素，形成兼具感官沉浸与智性趣味的听觉体验。

items.body: Review by Logan — Looking Beyond The Beautiful Space Out in the CountryThe short-form record tends to work on a different logic than a full LP. I value EPs that carry their own weight as intentional, self-contained pieces rather than just acting as a way to repackage existing music for sale.Much like a short film, an EP can use its brevity to settle into a specific mood or texture, without needing to extend those ideas across the length of a full studio album.Godspeed You Black Emperor!'s Slow Riot for New Zero Kanada does this well, letting tracks like "Moya" and "BBF3" create a heavy and distinct presence in under thirty minutes. Boards of Canada seems to approach the format similarly. A record like In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country does not feel like leftover tracks -- it works as an independent soundscape where the brief runtime is used for deliberate atmosphere.An important aspect of In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country is that these tracks do not appear on other major releases, which makes the EP an essential piece of their discography rather than a minor supplement. It stands out as one of my very favourite EPs. Listening to it highlights a beautiful and mysterious ambient density built on a sort of melancholy, discomforting and comforting nostalgia.I especially adore the tracks "Kid for Today" and "In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country" but I think the whole record is superb taken as a whole. "Zoetrope" did not at first appeal much, but during consecutive listens I got how its minimalist ambience worked with and added to the rest of the release. It helps to demonstrate how their use of repetitive, cyclical structures can reveal deeper qualities when one sits with the textures over a period of time. That highlights to me how a track can reward patience.I give it 5 stars as one of my most essential EPs.
items._genre: ambient / electronic / IDM / downtempo
items._cn_summary: 这张EP以极简的篇幅构建了一个独立自足的声音空间，避免了拼凑旧作的嫌疑。评论者将其与Godspeed You! Black Emperor!的Slow Riot相提并论，认为短格式作品可以通过克制时长来营造特定氛围与质感。整张作品建立在怀旧、忧郁、不安与慰藉交织的情绪密度之上，循环往复的极简结构在反复聆听中逐渐显露出深层肌理，考验听者的耐心与沉浸度。评论者尤其推崇Kid for Today与同名曲In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country，而最初并不感兴趣的Zoetrope也在多次聆听后展现了其极简氛围与整体的呼应关系。该EP收录的曲目未见于其他主要作品，因此成为乐队唱片体系中的关键一环，作为独立厂牌发行的ambient电子短篇，在氛围营造与结构实验之间取得了平衡。

items.excerpt: The ID:UD Senior Staff will spare no expense and forsake no opportunity to check out shows related to Our Thing and report back to you, the concerned and engaged reader and listener. Alex headed out to Toronto for the weekend in order to finally see the oft-promised, never delivered (until now) miracle of a live Tear Garden set, while Bruce stayed closer to home and checked out the Vancouver instalment of the Immortalis tour, featuring Past Self, Pink Stiletto, ET, Ringinger, and Covert Forces.
items.body: The ID:UD Senior Staff will spare no expense and forsake no opportunity to check out shows related to Our Thing and report back to you, the concerned and engaged reader and listener. Alex headed out to Toronto for the weekend in order to finally see the oft-promised, never delivered (until now) miracle of a live Tear Garden set, while Bruce stayed closer to home and checked out the Vancouver instalment of the Immortalis tour, featuring Past Self, Pink Stiletto, ET, Ringinger, and Covert Forces. We’ll have a full discussion of both nights on this week’s podcast. Okay, admittedly these are shows we’d still be going to even if we didn’t run a website and podcast dedicated to this biz, but we might as well make a meal of it, no? On with this week’s tracks. The Sick Man Of Europe Statiqbloom, “A Grief Observed” Votive, the latest three-track release from now veteran electro-industrial cum dark techno project Statiqbloom does a nice job of triangulating most of the sounds Fade Kainer’s employed under that name over the past decade, from murky half-time power electronics on “Cut The Vine” to more straightforward distorted kicks on “Erased”. But despite its very brief run-time, it’s the sickly acidic programming of “A Grief Observed”, crawling beneath Kainer’s mutters which is reminding us of why we’ve loved his psychedelic approach to vintage post-industrial for so long. Votive by Statiqbloom The Sick Man of Europe, “Apathy” Some pleasingly minimal but still melodic synth action from the UK’s Sick Man of Europe sure is hitting the spot right now. Maybe it’s the insistent drum programming, or the beleeping bass and synthwork, or the punky feedback on the lead, but the contrast between those elements and the frustration and anger of the lyrics certainly gives this one some juice. The Intermittent Signal by The Sick Man Of Europe Nick Viola, “Soft Brutalism” Nick Viola’s name should ring a bell to regular readers, either for his excellent work as Fractured Transmission or his role in the defunct Death Camp Audio clique releases from about a decade back (or his role in US supergroup HexRx, going back further), but a new EP under his own name functions as a good reintroduction to the read on dark techno he’s been working on in recent years. Dense and icy washes of distortion keep the kicks from ever running riot and pushing the subtler cyber programming out of the frame. Soft Brutalism by Nick Viola ᚾᛟᚢ, “Break Like Frost” Nothing Nordvargr finds while digging into his archives is likely to be “pleasant” in any traditional sense of the word. But it’s interesting to hear something like this pulled from the vaults, the first (so far as we can determine) release under the “ᚾᛟᚢ” name, clarifying the nominative distinction between Nordvargr and Trepaneringsritualen’s Thomas Martin Ekelund in their collaborative ᚾᛟᚢ II // ᚦᛟᚦ ᚷᛁᚷ project. Regardless of name or origin the icy mood of this piece’s drifts of death industrial and dark ambient soundscapes are apparent from the moment it begins even without looking at its title, with some classic lo-fi cassette style recording. Trollkorset by ᚾᛟᚢ Then Comes Silence, “Remaker Redeemer” Sweden’s Then Comes Silence make the kind of muscly, synth-inflected goth rock that has never truly gone out of style in Europe. And to their credit, they do it well; where so many acts who attempt the style have neither the vocal charisma nor the hooks to pull it off, TCS has plenty of both to spare. “Remaker Redeemer” has all kinds of mood and atmosphere, but doesn’t skimp on a big jump up chorus, accented by some grindy basswork and syncopated drums that make it fit for the club or the headphones. Requiem Ballroom by THEN COMES SILENCE Ye Gods, “Outlier (single edit)” Oh, to live in a world where songs like Ye Gods’ “Outlier” could be actual radio play singles. Kidding aside, we’re obviously huge fans of Antoni Maiovvi’s work, especially in the sprawling and conceptual esoteric canvas that the producer has made of Ye Gods (hear our interview from last year here), and this cut is no exception. It’s rhythmic, weird, lovely and unnerving, and often both at the same time. New EP Los comes out mid-October, mark it on your halloween calendars. Los by Ye Gods The post Tracks: October 5th, 2027 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评以节目推荐形式串联了四组地下电子/工业音乐人的近期作品。Statiqbloom 的《A Grief Observed》以病态酸涩的合成器编程配合人声低语，展现其迷幻式后工业手法；英国组合 The Sick Man of Europe 走极简但旋律化的合成器路线，鼓机与刺耳反馈形成情绪张力对比；Nick Viola 在新 EP 中以密集失真铺陈冰冽质感，压制鼓机以保留微妙赛博编程层次；ᚾᛟᚢ 则是 Nordvargr 从档案中挖掘出的早期录音，澄清了他与 Trepaneringsritualen 项目之间的名义区分。整体聚焦于小型独立厂牌的暗潮与工业电子场景，评论简洁但对每件作品的音色细节与制作手法有具体技术性描述。

items.body: Tracing Back The Radiance is Jefre Cantu-Ledesma’s third full-length release on Mexican Summer. This time around, he’s a long way from his more recent pop-oriented material, opting instead for gleaming, slow meditations. Cantu-Ledesma enters a spacious and reflective place which is more about the creation of an optimistic atmosphere and less about the pursuit of melodic development, although contrails of melody do emerge. The album has a stellar cast of musicians: John Also Bennett, Marilu Donavan, Chuck Johnson, Gregg Kowalsky, Mary Lattimore, David Moore, Meara O’Reilly, Jonathan Sielaff, Roger Tellier Craig, and Christopher Tignor are all a part of its sculpted landscape, but the music never feels cluttered. Instead, it retains its open environment and friendly nature with an emphasis on texture and delicacy in movement. Space is paramount, even with the presence of vibraphone, processing, flute, pedal steel, synthesizer, piano, organ, and voice. The album gestated for a year, and its smooth curves are a testament to its lengthy period of creation. Patience and meticulous study has paid off. Tracing Back The Radiance reshapes and loosens the meaning and possibilities of discourse, communication, and collaboration, enabling a more open, flexible, and dynamic approach. The multi-layered world of sound is as hopeful as a shaft of morning sunlight, young and open to change. From all corners of North America (significant in its symbolism), the ensemble link up, joining hands across the nation. All of its tones are equal, and each one forms a chain, with one leading and then another following, the next being promoted and then following its predecessor, creating both ladders and waterfalls. What’s really astonishing is the album’s cohesiveness. All of the artists are on the same page, understanding the momentum to the point of telepathy, resulting in peaceful instrumentals. Suffused with lightness, floating like bubbles of air as they lessen the gap between earth and sky, and basking in the warmth of the sun, Tracing Back The Radiance is smooth sailing. In 2019, this kind of balm is sorely needed. Tracing Back The Radiance by Jefre Cantu-Ledesma www.jefrecantu-ledesma.bandcamp.com
items._genre: ambient / drone / modern composition / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这是Jefre Cantu-Ledesma在Mexican Summer厂牌发行的第三张全长专辑，汇聚了横跨北美的十余位音乐人共同参与录制。作品以缓慢而发光的冥想式声响为核心，注重空间感与质感的细腻雕琢，借助颤音琴、长笛、踏板钢吉他、合成器、钢琴、管风琴与人声等多元乐器，在保持开放氛围的同时避免了声音的拥挤。经过长达一年的孕育期，专辑呈现出流畅而圆融的曲线，各乐手之间展现出近乎心灵感通的默契，使所有音色形成平等的链条彼此呼应。整体音乐如晨光般温暖而充满希望，在器乐铺陈中缩减了大地与天空之间的距离，以轻盈漂浮的姿态探索沟通与协作的开放可能。

items.body: “We fear the abyss called death because of a lack of imagination. Give up your death! Other dimensions exist beyond this material world, and the people there are shining a light for us to follow” Around the time of Hallowe’en and Dia de los Muertos, the spirit world shuffles towards the living, and its inhabitants carry glowing lanterns to light the way. As afternoons succumb to longer nights, the decidedly chilly winds of November require thicker coats as they rattle the bones, and the frights of October fade away. Some spirits still linger; they make themselves known through Tape Loop Orchestra’s music, like the senile smell of a perfume from the 1940’s. Some of them take up residence inside The Invisibles, working their way into the very fabric of the music, but other phantoms share the space, too. They’re artificially created, spooling out of a recurring nightmare’s webbed strands and surreal scenarios. The notes are fragile and transparent, and an almost ethereal atmosphere blows over the music like a cloud of cigarette smoke. Right from the off, the vocals of Beth Roberts haunt The Invisibles, settling down in a cool space, as if seated on the periphery of a dead nightclub. Shrouded in fog, the stalker that we call death suspends itself over the music, circling its next, clueless victim like a grotesque disco ball. Her striking lyricism soon loops and decays, and like a disintegrating memory her sturdy and strong voice begins to lose its once-reliable, storm-proof sound. It slowly shrinks and wastes away, like an underused muscle, losing its physicality, becoming spirit. Her held notes are like long strands of ectoplasm that so famously spluttered out of the mouth during private séances in the Victorian era. And the music is covered in a swollen layer of century-old dust, its skin permanently mummified. The processed strings try to emit their own kind of weak radiance – they’re used to shining brightly – but even these have grown pale. Something intangible rubs against the music, making The Invisibles less of a faked episode of Most Haunted and more of an authentic paranormal investigation. Her voice chants its hymn, spreading as if from a localized infection. When the vocals fade away, they drift into the unknown and their absence creates a presence. The strings slowly swell, swirling and roiling in the murky tempest that engulfs life and death. The notes waver, staggering through the ambient-lit fog, zombie-like. They wear a cloak, and they drape themselves over the fog. On Side Two, the notes are even thinner. The ice is crackling in the background, and the tones are close to disintegrating. An angelic chorus appears, trying to lift the music up and embalming it with its layers of vocal honey. Over the years, so many people have claimed to have seen a tunnel of white light as their own near-death experiences were recounted, and now this light hovers over the music. The disembodied spirit looks down on a temporary vessel it used to call home. All the saints are here, and it doesn’t matter if they’re the illusions of a misfiring brain. They’re with you, and that’s what matters. Death stalks the music as the misty-grey tones sit underneath the vocals, acting like lamp posts that illuminate inner circles of safe light to counteract a world perpetually suffocated by darkness and cruelty. The music isn’t here to hurt. It’s like a lantern, lighting the way for a smooth, liquid returning. Available through Boomkat on 11.11.16 www.oursmallideas.tumblr.com

items._cn_summary: Tape Loop Orchestra 的《The Invisibles》以磁带环路为核心手法，将人声、处理过的弦乐与嗡鸣质感融合，构建出一种弥漫着鬼魂气息的声场。Beth Roberts 的声线在循环与衰减中逐渐失去物质性，仿佛从有形的肉身过渡为飘忽的灵体，与维多利亚时代降灵会中的异象形成呼应。弦乐在阴沉音景中微弱地发光，却又被百年尘埃所覆盖，始终无法完全穿透雾霭。B 面的旋律愈发稀薄，冰冷的环境声响与天使般的合唱交替出现，模拟濒死体验中那道白光的意象。整体而言，专辑以万圣节与亡灵节为文化语境，将磁带音乐的物理损耗转化为超自然主题的隐喻，模糊了声音、记忆与灵性之间的边界。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国裔肯尼亚鼓手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成二人组Odd Okoddo，并联合八十三岁的传统肯尼亚歌手Ogoya Nengo共同完成。评论聚焦于三方的声音协作：Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手掌打击乐与鼓组构建电子律动基底，而Nengo与Ratengo的人声则在东肯尼亚dodo传统声乐框架中交织呼应。文中以《Bara》和《Sarah》两首作品为例，详述了合成复节奏如何逐层渗入人声织体，最终形成有机整体的过程。评论将这类音乐置于更广泛的全球folktronica语境中，与Chouk Bwa及Nyege Nyege厂牌作品并置讨论，强调其文化交融特质——传统根基与前卫声响并行而不互相覆盖。

items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.

items._genre: avant-garde / experimental / ambient / contemporary classical / protest
items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz携改名后的United States of Alchemy回归，与前卫作曲家Paladino及诗人Ferrari合作推出专辑《Songs of Compassion》。十一首作品以钢琴为核心，穿插弦乐、木管与合成器音色，采用非线性的调式与和声结构，远离西方传统功能和声体系，呈现冥想般的声景氛围。旋律如意识流般起伏，不遵循常规音阶进行，而是强调每个歌词的语义重量。Moskowitz的演唱沉稳老练，钢琴则如希腊戏剧中的歌队般对叙事进行评注。歌词延续1960年代抗议歌曲传统，既有对当下政治极化与威权主义的尖锐批判，如《Pale Wanderer》与《Charlottesville》，也有关于死亡与人在宇宙中位置的沉思。整体呈现高远却不失真诚的哲学姿态。

items.body: Progressive rock can be defined in many ways but one of my favorites is with the tension between a frenetic, jittery energy and sweet, soothing melody. Think King Crimson, where you never know which the band will choose from and often get both: the staccato, chopped up riff, or the dreamy, pleasing melody. This creates a tension, a contrast between the two sounds that, when wielded well, generates an inimitable energy and mood. Sans Froid are experts at doing just that, marrying dense, complex, unpredictable instrumentation and unexpected vocal phrases with a "classic" melodic approach. The end result is Back Into the Womb, an album that covers the spaces between heavy, muscular progressive rock and fragile, warm art rock."Go On", the track which opens the album, leaves us very little space before it introduces the first aspect of this sound. This is the track's excellent combo of the main guitar riff, punchy drums, and punctual bass. It creates that off-kilter vibe I mentioned earlier, that jittery feeling. The vocals follow suit but also quickly usher in the other mood, a more classical, melodic kind of approach on the track's first bridge. But here's the thing - that back and forth is not maintained. There is no A/B/A/B/C structure to this track. It gets smashed to pieces by this sudden turn that the instruments and especially the vocals take around at two minutes and fifteen. It's hard to overstate how much I love what happens there: the initially repetitive but then exquisitely explosive vocals, the deconstructed guitar line, and then the return of the big, muscular main riff.The entire album is filled with these ideas, refusing to choose one style and instead hopping between groove, experimentation, emotiveness, abrasiveness and more. Throughout, the vocals lead the way. They're incredible, again channeling that contrast we opened on. Their basic timbre is very sweet but it often gets augmented by a throaty, full approach that works exceedingly well with the album's basic groove. But, as evinced on "Go On", Sans Froid are happy to manipulate them further, sometimes casting them in sweeping, "traditional" choruses and sometimes chopping them up and deploying them in non-standard ways while at others setting them as a melancholic, emotive, gentle dirge. The result is that their sound is the centerpiece of the album, tying everything together, but never becoming obvious or background noise.Which also brings us, at the outset, full circle to the album's other brilliance: its production. Every instrument is meticulously placed where it needs to be and even on the album's busiest passages, every comes through beautifully. The bass is at the bottom but it never slips, always audible in its support. The drums hit very hard right where they should without overwhelming anything else. And the guitars are at time noisy and beefy but at others poignantly sharp and incisiveness. It serves to bring Sans Froid's ambition, which is substantial, to exquisite execution, bringing forth the musical vision in beautiful light. Fans of progressive rock know how hard this is to achieve and also know the joy of discovering an album which does this well, an intricate album whose sound matches its composition. Back Into the Womb is that and more, an album from a band which I knew nothing about that does everything I love progressive rock for. Back into the Womb by Sans Froid

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑在密集复杂、不可预测的器乐编排与经典旋律之间构建张力，融合了重型前卫摇滚的肌理与脆弱温暖的艺术摇滚气质。开场曲在前段稳定的节奏型与突发的爆发性人声、解构式吉他之间快速切换，拒绝固定结构，不断在律动、实验、情绪化与尖锐质感间跳跃。人声是专辑的核心纽带，基本音色甜美但时常转为厚重的喉音处理，既承担传统合唱段也以非标准方式切碎重组。制作层面各乐器位置精心布置，鼓击有力不喧宾夺主，贝斯沉稳支撑，吉他在噪音与锐利间游走，整体混音在密集段落仍保持清晰可辨。这种在结构中融入即兴式突变与情绪对比的写法，与学院派听众对非常规结构与声音探索的偏好高度契合。

items._cn_summary: 7FO新作延续其一贯的怪诞风格，从「道边拾石突然碎裂」这一记忆碎片出发，构建出奇异却亲和的听觉空间。专辑以新世纪的漂浮感作为氛围入口，融合电子质感与即兴元素，营造出人声与音色交错的音景。该作延续前作《Water Falls Into A Blank》的脉络，后者刚获海外重发许可，可见其声音美学在国际语境中的再发现。音乐在陌生感与亲近感之间找到平衡点——既是难以归类的实验声响，又具备某种温度，让听者沉浸于其构筑的声场之中。发行厂牌EM为日本独立厂牌，规模小众，保持了艺术家表达的独立性。

items.body: Look at all those people! Everything seems bigger on Hour‘s newest album. There are fourteen people in the ensemble (four missing the photo shoot). The Bandcamp description is a thousand words long. The album is offered on black vinyl, colored vinyl, deluxe CD and promo CD. So why does Ghost Bridge sound so much smaller and more intimate ~ even more so than Subminiature? The answers are the arrangements and the brevity. On Ghost Bridge, the Philly ensemble led by Michael Cormier-O’Leary continues its slow shift from post-rock to modern composition. The pieces – and by extension, the instruments – are given more room to breathe. A half dozen tracks unfold in a concise 36 minutes. Late in the set, a vocal selection slows the pace to a pleasant crawl. Hour is still more Rachel’s than Low, but is carving out a niche at a pace similar to that of a stream cutting channels in stone. The title is taken from an “unrealized movie concept” about a disappearing and reappearing bridge. From this prompt, the album muses on tragedies, ghosts and the nature of the soul. Over a quarter of the album is devoted to the title track, whose very length suggests it bears the specter of post-rock. Solo piano is joined by light drums, then vibraphone, then all the other instruments in time, gathering like a crowd at a wake, forming layers of consolation, adding confidence and strength until the grief itself becomes a ghost. The end is a soft mist of notes, a few stragglers staying behind to whisper to the piano before they all go home. But where did it all begin? “Pearls” is the opening track, proceeding from a series of repeated notes to engage in happy permutations. Little sorrow can be intuited here; instead the starting point is a breezy, carefree day, filled with horse-drawn carriages and hot air balloons until the full stop at the three-minute mark, when darker clouds can be seen on the horizon: not yet here, but on their way. The pianist stumbles; the string players look up; the concentration of the percussionist is disrupted. The flautist resets the mood: the sorrow has not yet approached, so let us savor the now. The sedate ending sets up “Centralia,” a series of layered phrases that circle back and repeat like recurring thoughts or the motivational sentences of friends. Only after “Ghost Bridge” does “Sky Is Blue” emerge, perfectly placed as the first track on Side B, albeit jarring in the digital and CD versions. The lyrics, sung by Heeyoon Won, reveal it to be an extensive message from the great beyond, delivered by a loved one who is completely okay, filled with perspective, encouragement and hope. Should one not own the LP, we recommend moving “Sky Is Blue” to the finale. Given this sequencing, “So Long Without a Word” slips into the void at the end of “Ghost Bridge,” its melodic tones speaking directly to the soul, the full stop now at 2:00, followed by increasing energy and resolve. A third phase begins two minutes later with insistent, cinematic strums, then a playful series of shifts, jazz to chamber and back, like a playground ball. “Sonny” returns the timbre to post-rock and the mood to reflective yet ebullient, the ghost bridge now reappearing, the path between heaven and earth secure. (Richard Allen)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由十四人编制的大型室内乐团演绎，从后摇滚缓慢转向现代作曲领域。乐评指出编曲的精炼与短小的篇幅赋予了作品私密感，尽管阵容庞大却营造出亲密氛围。专辑围绕一座虚幻之桥的意象展开，探讨悲剧、幽灵与灵魂本质等主题。曲目以层叠方式展开乐器组合，从独奏钢琴逐步加入鼓、颤音琴及其他乐器，形成安慰与力量的层次。歌词曲目"Sky Is Blue"作为亡者跨越的讯息出现，带来希望与鼓励的视角。乐评建议非黑胶听众将该曲移至末尾以获得更佳的情感弧线。整体呈现学院派室内乐气质，融合后摇滚的动态展开与现代作曲的结构意识。

items.body: Neubauten's uncompromising debut album ‘Kollaps’ is 45 years old. Jeremy Allen explores the bombed-out terrain of their West Berlin and wonders if, despite the penurious conditions, it was easier to make art then Feral musicians emerging from the rubble of bombed-out West Berlin (as composer György Ligeti described it, "a surrealist cage in which all those inside are free") and creating themselves out of their own blood and guts very much feels like a tale from another age. In a world of coffee shop startups, utilitarian computer software and ersatz bedroom electronica as aural wallpaper, building your own percussive instruments from scrap might seem primitive, complex, redundant even. items.body: Anyankofo means friends in Fante, and the Danish seven-piece Total Hip Replacement have been collecting them in Ghana since a mini-tour there in 2013. In the winter of 2021 they formed a nine-piece band in Accra with Ghanaian highlife, reggae and gospel musicians and gave it that name, which also titles the album the group recorded at Kwame Yeboah‘s Kwashibu studio, released in 2022. A later trip to Ghana took them to Kumasi, the Ashanti capital and one of highlife’s strongholds, and a week of jamming there with players from Frafra gospel singer Florence Adooni‘s band and with Nsoroma of Accra highlife band Santrofi produced “The Search”. It is the latest single ahead of the album Ehum, and the band say it holds on to the improvised feel of the jams. The song is about hunting for purpose in a society that keeps speeding up, where the pressure to get ahead alone costs people their connection to each other. Singer and trombonist Victor West Hosbond fronts the band’s horn section, the signature of their sound, and on this single it rides a highlife rhythm. The band describe the mood they chased as “the hopeful spot between melancholy and euphoria“. They filmed the video over a couple of days at an old farmhouse in France during this summer’s tour, with Nell Le Corre behind the camera. Ehum, which the band translate as storm, comes out on 27 November with Ivorian reggae singer Tiken Jah Fakoly among the guests. A West African run through Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana opens the tour, then Danish dates follow from February into April, among them ALICE in Copenhagen on 26 February and Aarhus on 27 March. Stream “The Search” HERE and pre-order Ehum through THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Total Hip Replacement – The Search appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Band: Antropoceno | Album: No Ritmo da Terra | Genre: Post-rock | Bandcamp The newest release from this experimental Brazilian act is a harsh and uncompromising record. Taking cues from glitch, avant-garde metal, and native folk, and with lyrics in Portuguese, Tupi, and Yoruba, No Ritmo da Terra is a truly autochthonous Brazilian album. The sound is often maximal, bursting with shining synths, biting guitars and rattling percussion.  Score: 77/100 Band: Beware of Gods | Album: Upon Whom the Last Light Descends III: Behead the Oracle | Genre: Sludge metal, Post-metal | Bandcamp Beware of Gods’ latest album is full of groovy riffs and punishing walls of biting distortion. This band deftly uses texture and atmosphere to paint pictures, and there are a lot of creative and unorthodox choices in how passages and phrases are composed. The sci-fi story the album tells meshes well with the oppressive soundscapes, and this is an instance of things like sound effects and spoken dialogue adding to the effect of the record. Score: 75/100 Band: Haken | Album: in a fever dream | Genre: Progressive metal | Bandcamp This is the most I’ve enjoyed a Haken release since The Mountain. On Haken’s last few LPs, the band had leaned into a form of melodic djent, which, while dazzlingly technical, lacked anything all that memorable, at least to my ear. This new EP sees them take a step back from that and dip their toes back into more Dream Theater-style prog metal. This isn’t just the blatant DT worship of their first two records, though. The band has matured their sound and put their own unique stamp on things. They also include some great moody alt-rock and electronic flourishes, a la Porcupine Tree/Steven Wilson. Score: 85/100 Band: Kolm | Album: Yūgen | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp I like Kolm’s 2018 debut, Umbra, but it is also some of the most blatant and unashamed Tool worship I’ve ever heard. Eight years later, this L.A.-based trio is back with their sophomore album, Yūgen. Yūgen is still obviously deeply indebted to Tool, but the band has diversified their sound a bit. Cynic jumps out as an obvious influence, and they’ve also developed their songwriting and arrangements to be more uniquely their own. My main complaint here is that this is a very long record. A number of riffs and ideas feel drawn out, and the band definitely could have tightened things up. Beyond that, there are a lot of great textures, and the bandmembers are clearly skilled musicians. There are some nice electronic interludes, too. Ignoring the bloat, there’s a lot of good music here. Score: 71/100 Band: Otobo | Album: Inside Machines | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp Otobo is a trio from Albany, NY, that plays a crunchy, aggressive band of progressive rock heavily influenced by alt-rock. The songs are all manageable lengths with minimal bloat, but they still contain exciting, dynamic composition. Noise rock, post-punk, and math rock get their turns in the spotlight, too. Otobo does a great job at keeping textures varied, and there’s a skilled balance of complex artiness and enjoyable hooks. The album does lose a bit of steam near the end, but it’s still solid overall. Score: 74/100 Band: Panopticon | Album: Det Hjemsøkte Hjertet | Genre: Post-metal | Bandcamp Billed as a conclusion to a trilogy of records (the others being …And Again into the Light and Rime of Memory), Det Hjemsøkte Hjertet, is another powerful and affecting release in Pantopicon’s discography. The soundscapes swell and bristle, exploding with scouring-yet-abstract black metal riffs. Bluegrass and other forms of American folk music are prominent. Panopticon has a definite sound, so there’s only so much that can be said here that wouldn’t just be describing other records. But this features many of the band’s strongest elements. Score: 82/100

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: Analog Africa厂牌推出的第44号发行，收录贝宁传奇乐队Orchestre Poly-Rythmo与创作人Antoine Dougbé在1977至1982年的合作录音。Dougbé以拍腿打出Cavacha节奏著称，这一律动由鼓手Belobi Meridjo从火车节奏中提炼，后席卷刚果流行乐坛。作为伏都教信仰者，Dougbé的音乐笼罩着神秘仪式色彩，他只与Poly-Rythmo合作，因为后者能精准呈现他所需的声音质感。专辑横跨1970年代末至1980年代初，录音呈现明显的时代质感：吉他带有塑料光泽，合成器开始大量渗透。音乐根源上更明显地融入了古巴son的影响，辅以刚果伦巴的摇摆律动，作品如《Ma Won Min Towe Leo》以合成器铺垫为底，闪烁的吉他咬合在高帽驱动的律动之上，乐手在出型上相互竞逐后又重新汇聚。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队以废弃材料自制乐器（tassofons、tilofons、kitchenofon 等），用这些自制乐器演奏出令人惊叹的丰富音质，每件乐器都意外地音准准确、音色饱满。专辑融合了克莱兹默、昆比亚、非洲节拍、桑巴和中东风等多种音乐风格，每首曲目对应不同的文化语汇：单簧管演绎克莱兹默曲调、长笛承载拉丁旋律、木鱼与沙锤营造 afrobeat 氛围。乐队在传统曲式基础上加入大量即兴段落，展现出高超的演奏技巧。自制乐器的概念本身具有强烈的实验与环保意味，跨越文化边界的音乐组织方式体现了世界音乐的多元融合理念，同时也提醒人们音乐诞生于人类对声音的热爱，不受限于乐器的物质形态。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 挪威Camilla Hole Trio在《Langs》中将高音萨克斯与挪威西部传统舞蹈曲调相融合，同时引入模块化合成器与颤音琴的色彩层。乐评聚焦开场曲《Springleik》，展示三重奏成员角色不断流动互换的演奏方式：低音提琴手Kalman与鼓手Nesheim首先以节奏支撑Hole的旋律，随后Kalman以贝斯接过旋律线并与萨克斯齐奏，Nesheim则进一步拓展节奏维度，使整体走向更为即兴的方向。相比前作《Eventyrferd》中科幻合成器与传统素材的大胆嫁接，《Langs》更回归地面，但仍延续了超越本国本民族民间音乐的探索路线。三位乐手在即兴框架下对民谣素材进行解构与重组，体现了北欧爵士特有的克制与开放并存的美学气质。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张由瑞典小提琴家与两位挪威乐手组成的跨国三重奏专辑，以斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲素材为出发点进行解构与重塑。三位音乐家各自拥有跨越民谣、学院与世界音乐领域的背景：一位深耕瑞典民间音乐并不断探索风格融合，一位从七十年代挪威先锋跨界乐队走来、习惯将竖笛与萨克斯、袋管等域外乐器并置，另一位则以鼓手与作曲人身份模糊流派边界。在他们的演绎下，传统舞曲素材不再为舞蹈服务，更接近室内乐式的亲密对话——三件乐器相互呼应、碎裂、重组，挖掘旋律表面之下更幽暗的意涵。编曲上以竖笛主奏旋律为主，辅以小提琴的肌理铺底与打击乐的细碎点缀，整体氛围神秘而内省，适合对民谣实验化处理与北欧声音美学感兴趣的听众。
